c.tagline: The Friendly City — Algoa Bay beaches and gateway to Addo's elephants.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis must be booked by phone or app rather than hailed in the street; Uber and Bolt are the usual choice, while shared minibus taxis run fixed routes cheaply for locals.

emergency.note: From a mobile phone 112 connects to all emergency services; 10111 is the police and 10177 is the ambulance service.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Richmond Hill: Stanley Street, Richmond Hill, Port Elizabeth

avoid.reason: Caution in the CBD and townships; muggings at night

hood_desc: The prime seaside base along Marine Drive, with Hobie and Pollok beaches, Nelson Mandela University, the Boardwalk casino-and-dining complex and most of the city's beachfront hotels.
A beachfront neighbourhood centred on Kings Beach and the promenade, with the harbour close by; a classic, relaxed seaside stay a short hop from the centre.
The historic British-colonial core around the Donkin Reserve, the Campanile bell tower and the Route 67 public-art trail; rich in heritage but quiet after business hours.
A revived hilltop district above the centre, best known for the Stanley Street strip of trendy restaurants, cafés and bars — the city's go-to for eating out and nightlife.
A leafy, affluent inland suburb of large homes and guesthouses next to the airport, offering a quiet, green base a short drive from both the beaches and the centre.
lodging: Protea Hotel by Marriott Port Elizabeth Marine

water.note: Tap water is treated and generally safe, though drought restrictions can affect supply.

transit.hours: Algoa buses run mainly on weekday commuter schedules (roughly 6 AM to 6 PM) with very limited evening and weekend service; informal minibus taxis run longer hours.
transit.pay: Algoa buses take cash and rechargeable fare cards; minibus taxis are cash-only, paid to the driver at fixed route fares.
transit.note: Public transport is limited and the city is car-dependent. The Algoa Bus Company runs scheduled routes from Market Square, supplemented by informal minibus taxis; a planned bus-rapid-transit system remains largely unfinished, so most visitors use Uber/Bolt or rent a car.

bus: Intercity coaches (Intercape and others) & minibus taxis

transit.m: Metered taxi to the city centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: ~10-15% at restaurants and for guides; tip petrol attendants and informal car guards a few rand.

landmarks: Donkin Reserve
A lighthouse, memorial pyramid and towering flag mark this hillside park, centerpiece of the Route 67 artworks celebrating Nelson Mandela's legacy.
Route 67
Sixty-seven public artworks, one for each year of Mandela's public life, thread mosaic stairways and murals through the city's historic heart.
Shark Rock Pier and Hobie Beach
Gqeberha's postcard pier juts from golden Hobie Beach, prime territory for sunrise photographs, sailing and the friendly city's famous watersports.
The Campanile
This 52-meter brick bell tower of 1923 commemorates the landing of the 1820 Settlers, with a 23-bell carillon and viewing gallery.
Fort Frederick
Built in 1799 above the Baakens River mouth, this small stone fort guarded the bay for Britain yet never fired a shot in anger.
St George's Park
South Africa's oldest cricket ground, host of the first Test match on African soil in 1889, anchors this graceful Victorian park.
South End Museum
Photographs and recreated shopfronts movingly memorialize the vibrant multiracial South End district demolished under apartheid's Group Areas Act.
Nelson Mandela Metropolitan Art Museum
This bright gallery beside St George's Park showcases Eastern Cape artists, South African masters and British colonial-era works in rotating exhibitions.
Sardinia Bay
Wild dunes tumble onto an unspoiled Blue Flag beach west of the city, part of a marine reserve ideal for long walks and horse rides.
Bayworld
A beachfront complex in Humewood combining a natural history museum, oceanarium, and snake park focused on the Eastern Cape's marine and coastal life.

train.note: The weekly Shosholoza Meyl long-distance train links Port Elizabeth to Johannesburg via Bloemfontein; local Metrorail commuter services are limited.

bus.note: Intercity coaches (Intercape and others) link Port Elizabeth along the Garden Route to Cape Town (~10-11 hr) and eastward to East London and Durban, plus an overnight route to Johannesburg.

ferry.note: Port Elizabeth (Gqeberha) has a busy commercial harbour and the deep-water container terminal at Ngqura 20 km up the coast, but neither handles scheduled passenger ships, and South Africa has no coastal passenger ferry network. The only boats for visitors are Algoa Bay excursions from the Nelson Mandela Bay waterfront - harbour cruises and whale-, dolphin- and penguin-watching trips out towards St Croix and Bird Island, which land nowhere. There are no international sailings; cruise liners call occasionally but do not sell point-to-point passage.
